Nebraska Game and Parks Commission
2200 North 33rd Street / P.O. Box 30370 / Lincoln, Nebraska 68503
April 14, 1972
Mrs. Linda Proskovec
State Office of Planning and Programming
Box 94601
State Capitol
Lincoln, Nebraska 68509
Dear Mrs. Proskovec:
Following are our comments relating to the Draft Environmental Impact Statement for the Endangered Species Act of 1972 prepared by the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife Of U.S. Department of Interior on March 21, 1972.
The bill would make the taking of an endangered species a federal offense, and would in effect, remove listed species from state's jurisdiction. We are enclosing copies of our state laws which were passed to enable Nebraska to comply with and be consistent with the intent of the federal law, that of providing full protection to the threatened or endangered species of wildlife.
It would seem wise to model the bill as to place jurisdiction with the state (s) for protection of endangered resident species of wildlife unless that state (s) has not chacted state legislation consistent with the intent of the federal law. The individual states have considerably more enforcement personnel in the field devoted to the protection of fish and wildlife than does the federal government. Nebraska employs approximately 45 conservation officers, whereas, there are 3 (2 at the present time) federal management and enforcement officers assigned to Nebraska. It is true that most of the Nebraska conservation officers also have federal credentials, but it is considerably speedier and less involved to have a case tried in state court than in federal court. Thus from the standpoint of efficiency alone, it would seem wise to place primary authority for enforcing the laws on endangered resident wildlife species with the state (s) provided they have enacted the necessary laws.
